interpretation_limits: The NEA announcement confirms that the 2021-2025 hydrogeological report and a nitrate-risk field methodology were prepared; it does not expose the archive contents.
The linked RAR archive was not retrieved, hashed or inspected in this run.
No sample count, station count, analyte denominator, laboratory result, site coordinate or time-series row is asserted.

The 2026-06-24 law sets 2027-09-01 statutory milestones for relevant methodology approval and groundwater nitrate-risk-zone identification; the NEA announcement that a method was prepared does not prove formal approval or completion.

The announced report concerns groundwater monitoring and must not be merged with NFA food/drinking-water inspection records or treated as a distributed-network/bottled-water dataset without matrix confirmation.
Archive reuse and redistribution terms are not stated in the announcement and must be confirmed before publishing extracted data.
No nitrate threshold, local contamination prevalence, exposure level or public-health outcome is inferred from the announcement alone.

The WHO 2026 edition gives drinking-water guideline values of 50 mg/L as nitrate ion and 3 mg/L as nitrite ion, with a combined concentration-to-guideline ratio not exceeding 1; the chemical fact sheet lists its assessment date as 2016.
WHO guideline values are global health-based guidance, not Georgian law, and are not automatically applicable to raw groundwater unless its intended use and matrix are confirmed as drinking-water.

The WHO fact sheet identifies bottle-fed infants as the most sensitive population and notes that microbial contamination and gastrointestinal infection can increase methaemoglobinaemia risk when nitrate is present.
Excessive boiling can concentrate nitrate; boiling is not a nitrate-removal treatment.
